title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). The preregistered design (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) used gpt‑5‑mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer, N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes), and shared_initial_generation semantics (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered to both conditions). Confirmatory, artifact‑backed outcomes: complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples); Cohen's h = 0.0. We explicitly state up front that two preregistered design choices—shared_initial_generation semantics and reuse of the same deterministic validator as both runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer—produced a deterministic ceiling effect in this run that rendered the primary estimand uninformative for assessing generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics. We present the artifact‑backed execution and analysis, diagnose why the design produced a null outcome, and provide concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for benchmark hardening to expose generator×guard interactions in future runs.

sections.introduction:
Generative LLMs are increasingly proposed to translate natural‑language operator intent into device configurations and staged‑change workflows (canaries, progressive rollouts, rollback). Operational safety requires end‑to‑end evaluation that covers generation, deterministic verification, staged rollout semantics, rollback, and provenance. Prior work shows promise but also documents gaps in action‑aware evaluation and verifier integration. To probe the verifier’s practical effect on end‑to‑end safety we preregistered a paired confirmatory study (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) comparing a verifier‑augmented pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark.

Research question. Under ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1, does integrating a deterministic runtime validator with an LLM generator increase the paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline? The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded − baseline) and the confirmatory analysis and exclusion rules were frozen before execution.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation (N=400 pairs) using gpt‑5‑mini and a deterministic runtime validator, with archived execution and analysis artifacts that support all principal numbers. (2) An explicit, artifact‑grounded diagnosis showing that preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and validator/scorer conflation produced a deterministic ceiling effect that made the primary estimand uninformative. (3) Concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations to harden action‑aware benchmarks so future confirmatory runs can exercise blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors. (4) Reproducible artifacts and analysis seeds enabling exact replication of reported statistics.
sections.related_work: Intent→configuration translation and LLM‑driven NetOps have been demonstrated in prototypes and benchmarks (intent‑based configuration, PreConfig, GraphSynth), and IaC work shows verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair loops improve provisioning correctness (TerraFormer). Deterministic network verifiers and reachability tools detect configuration errors in offline and emulated settings. Agentic and tool‑augmented LLM workflows (ReAct, RAG, multi‑agent orchestrations) are applied to AIOps/NetOps but introduce new failure modes—hallucination, tool misuse, and miscalibrated confidence—that motivate runtime guardrails and staged deployment. Recent surveys highlight the absence of community‑standard action‑aware benchmarks that combine generation, runtime blocking, staged rollouts, rollback, and provenance; our work operationalizes a compact benchmark under strict preregistered semantics to probe verifier utility within these constraints.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen estimands. The study preregistration (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) fixed: N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes), generator = gpt‑5‑mini, runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer = deterministic_netops_validator_v5, shared_initial_generation = true (independent_condition_generation = false), and primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistration specified permutation‑based paired testing (two‑sided, α=0.05), an exact McNemar corroboration, and bootstrap percentile CIs for secondary summaries (seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000). Exclusion and missingness rules were frozen: deterministic three‑replay consistency checks determine automatic exclusions; no human adjudication is permitted.

Adapter semantics and shared generation. Execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family. Crucially, shared_initial_generation semantics requested a single deterministic LLM generation per task and delivered that identical candidate to both baseline and guarded episodes. This design isolates validator acceptance behavior on identical strings rather than exposing independent generator variance across conditions. The execution manifest records model_calls_used = 400 while completed episodes = 800; the reduced model_call count is a direct consequence of the shared‑generation semantics and is explained here to avoid confusion about model usage accounting.

Episode flow, validator policy, and repair rules. For each task the adapter requested a shared candidate from gpt‑5‑mini, delivered it to both episodes, and—only in the guarded episode—invoked deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which applied full intent‑constraint validation and, where configured, a single repair attempt per the preregistered repair policy. The same deterministic implementation served as both the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer. Validator traces include validation_before/after states, normalized configurations, difficulty metadata, and repair_applied flags for every episode; these traces are archived in the evidence bundle.

Deterministic replay and exclusion policy. The preregistration required deterministic three‑replay consistency checks: each agent+simulator pair (task+condition) was replayed three times; pairs with non‑identical replay outcomes or simulator errors would be flagged and excluded from primary analysis. The missingness plan specified automated exclusions only; flagged counts and reasons are reported in the analysis artifacts. In this run all deterministic consistency checks passed and no exclusions occurred.

Statistical analysis. The primary confirmatory test was a permutation‑based paired difference on safe‑deploy booleans, implemented by the preregistered paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor and reported as an exact permutation p‑value. An exact McNemar two‑sided test corroborates paired contingency outcomes. Secondary summaries included bootstrap percentile CIs for paired differences (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729). Cohen's h is reported for effect‑size interpretation. All analysis code, seeds, and artifacts are archived for reproducibility.

Deterministic three‑replay checks passed for all pairs; no automated exclusions were applied.

The paired contingency table shows n_11 = 400 and n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0, producing an observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. The preregistered permutation test returned p = 1.0; the exact McNemar two‑sided test returned p = 1.0. Bootstrapped 95% CI for the paired difference = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). Cohen's h = 0.0. These numbers are taken verbatim from the archived analysis artifacts.

Repair, rollback, and intervention diagnostics. No repairs or rollbacks were invoked in any episode (repair_applied = false across validator_trace entries). Representative validator traces show normalized configurations matched reference answers and validation_after.final_state equaled expected_final_state, explaining universal acceptance by the deterministic validator under shared candidates.

The archive contains per‑task difficulty metadata for all N=400 pairs; aggregated histograms may be derived from execution/task_manifest.jsonl in the artifact bundle. sections.discussion:
Why the primary estimand was uninformative (construct‑validity diagnosis). Two preregistered design choices caused a deterministic ceiling effect. First, shared_initial_generation semantics delivered identical generator outputs to baseline and guarded episodes, so any deterministic acceptance decision applied to that shared string produced identical outcomes across conditions. Second, the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer were identical deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementations; a verifier cannot disagree with itself on the same canonical input. When validator acceptance is deterministic and the generator candidate is identical, no discordant pairs are possible and the paired difference estimand necessarily equals zero. The observed null is therefore an artifact of frozen design choices rather than evidence that runtime verification is universally unnecessary.

Consequences for inferential power and interpretation. The preregistered power calculation assumed a non‑ceiling baseline and intra‑pair variance; those assumptions are violated here. The permutation and McNemar p = 1.0 correctly reflect identical outcomes. Researchers must therefore not interpret the null result as evidence that runtime guards lack utility in settings with independent generator variance, heterogeneous validators, adversarial seeds, or production noise.

Concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for benchmark hardening. We propose implementable changes, each supported by archived traces and execution semantics:

A. Independent per‑condition generation (independent_condition_generation = true). Delivering independently sampled generator outputs to each condition reintroduces generator variance and permits the guard to alter outcomes. Artifacts show how shared semantics reduced model_calls; switching to independent generation will increase model_calls but enables meaningful paired discordance.

B. Separate runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer implementations. Use heterogeneous scorers (or blind adjudicators) so acceptance decisions and post‑hoc scoring are independent; archived validator traces show that conflating roles forces concordance on identical inputs.

C. Controlled adversarial/perturbation seeding. Injecting a preregistered fraction of perturbed seeds (documented in the preregistration) guarantees baseline failure rate for power calculations; archived task difficulty labels provide plausible perturbation targets (very_hard patterns).

D. Enable and log repair invocations. Configure the adapter to allow multi‑attempt repairs and record repair proposals and outcomes in validator traces; in this run repair_applied = false but traces show repair hooks exist and can be exercised.

E. Difficulty‑stratified sampling or oversampling of very_hard patterns. The archived task manifest contains difficulty tags that permit stratified sampling to ensure sufficient error rates in the baseline for confirmatory detection.

Threats to validity and generalizability. Model and scope: single declared generator (gpt‑5‑mini) and single deterministic validator; results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity. Environment realism: the benchmark is synthetic and the simulator/validator do not capture production telemetry noise or adversarial actors. Construct validity: reusing the same deterministic validator for runtime guarding and post‑hoc scoring conflates acceptance and scoring. Adversarial robustness was not exercised and remains open for future study. Aggregated difficulty histograms for the full sample are available in the archived task manifest but were not embedded inline due to space; auditors can derive them directly from execution/task_manifest.jsonl.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline and an LLM‑only pipeline under compact action‑aware staging semantics. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and chosen generator+validator pairing every shared candidate satisfied the deterministic runtime validator, producing 100% safe‑deploy for both conditions (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). This deterministic ceiling effect is a direct artifact of preregistered design choices that removed opportunities for the runtime guard to alter outcomes; it does not imply that runtime verification lacks utility in heterogeneous, independently generated, adversarial, or production settings. We archive the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts so researchers can reproduce the run and use these artifacts to design hardened experiments (independent generation, adversarial seeding, heterogeneous validators) that exercise blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors in future confirmatory studies.

limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.

Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open for future work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting gap: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl; an aggregated histogram by difficulty level for the full sample is derivable from that manifest but was not embedded inline in the paper. Representative sample difficulty counts (first six tasks) are included in the Results section to illustrate benchmark diversity.
